# Preface {-}

## Who this book is for

I wrote this book for students in epidemiology or population health sciences working toward a PhD who want to move from associational thinking to causal thinking. I assume
you have had an introductory course in epidemiology and one in
biostatistics — you should be comfortable with concepts like confounding,
odds ratios, and hazard ratios, and with fitting a regression model. I do
not assume any prior exposure to causal inference as a formal framework,
and I do not assume any prior experience with R. Both are things we will
build up together, chapter by chapter.

## How the book works

The ideas in this book are easiest to learn when they are attached to a
real analysis rather than left as abstractions, so we will return
throughout to two running examples drawn from the National Ambulatory
Medical Care Survey (NAMCS). The first asks whether treatment with a
selective Cox-2 inhibitor, compared with a nonselective NSAID, changes
the risk of peptic ulcer disease. The second asks whether initiating a
statin changes the risk of a cardiovascular event, and brings in
follow-up time, censoring, and survival outcomes. As we work through
these examples, we will also build a small toolkit of R functions for
estimating causal effects — standardization, propensity score weighting,
censoring weights, and so on — that you will write once and then reuse,
and extend, in later chapters.

## Software

Appendix A walks through installing R, RStudio, and the packages this
book relies on, including a companion package that provides the NAMCS
example datasets in a de-identified, teaching-ready form. You can install
that package directly from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("alanbrookhart/NAMCS")
```

If you run into trouble at any point, Appendix A is the place to look
first.
